name: Credit Dataset
collection_method: Yes (Supervised Binary Classification). The dataset is fully labelled with the target column class, which categorizes loan applicants into two credit risk classes: good (low risk / creditworthy) and bad (high risk / likely to default)
known_limitations: • Class Imbalance & Asymmetric Cost: The dataset has a 70:30 class imbalance (700 good vs. 300 bad credit records). In real-world banking, misclassifying a bad customer as good (False Negative) is 5 times costlier than the reverse, so standard accuracy alone is misleading. • Small Sample Size: With only 1,000 instances and 20 features (which expand to ~60+ columns after one-hot encoding), complex models are prone to overfitting without cross-validation. • Historical & Currency Obsolescence: Collected in 1994 in Germany, monetary attributes like credit_amount are measured in Deutsche Marks (DM), making financial thresholds outdated for modern banking. • Sensitive / Demographic Attributes: Features such as personal_status (gender and marital status), age, and foreign_worker introduce demographic bias and fairness/compliance concerns if used directly in production lending models.
audit_findings: the test split has only 201 rows: accuracy 0.751 has a 95% interval of [0.687, 0.806] -- treat differences inside it as noise (more data, or repeated / cross-validated evaluation, before comparing models).
protected attribute column(s) ['age', 'credit_history', 'num_dependents', 'own_telephone'] were dropped before training (DROP_SENSITIVE_FEATURES) -- no fairness audit was run for them.
